## AC4 SATISFIED — verified on the specific jobs, not a run summary

Scheduled run `33985020312`, `headSha 4c9940348148` (current `origin/main`), which contains the
merged fix `9e6a0e436520`:

```
success  build-and-test / pytest (ubuntu-latest, py3.13)   <- gating cell
success  sweep (macos, full suite)
success  sweep (py3.14t)
success  sweep (py3.15)
success  sweep (py3.14)
success  sweep (declared lower-bound resolution)
success  sweep (external doc links)
in_progress  sweep (windows)                                <- AC5: out of scope
completed-and-failing jobs: 0
```

All three lanes named in AC4 pass. `sweep (windows)` was still running at the time of the check
and is explicitly out of scope per AC5 (continue-on-error, Windows epic).

Note on the merged sha: the change landed as `9e6a0e436520`, NOT as the pushed `459e1d1b099f`.
`main` is Rebase-If-Necessary, so Gerrit rebased on submit and rewrote the sha. Reachability was
therefore confirmed against the MERGED sha from a throwaway worktree at `origin/main`
(`git merge-base --is-ancestor 9e6a0e436520 HEAD` -> yes; `rebar verify-commit-ticket --rev
9e6a0e436520` -> `OK - resolved ae96-72a9-8145-4c85`). Checking `is-ancestor` against the pushed
sha reports a FALSE NEGATIVE; that hazard is now filed separately as
`felicific-blueribbon-kitty`.

## Close class: `regression` — established by bisecting the lane signal, not assumed

The failing test `test_reconcile_once_threads_composed_runtime_transport_into_apply` was
introduced 2026-08-18 by `40b8ac829588` and never modified since, which would suggest the defect
was latent for 18 days. **That is not what happened.** The non-editable sweep lanes were GREEN
five hours before the first failure:

```
run 33935191588  2026-09-05T01:07  sha e510c64dbcb6   macos/py3.14t/py3.15 = success
run 33950878570  2026-09-05T06:49  sha a33333b8709a   macos/py3.14t/py3.15 = FAILURE
```

So the lanes regressed inside `e510c64dbcb6..a33333b8709a` (18 commits). Hence `regression`
rather than `preexisting`.

## Trigger candidate — recorded as a LEAD, deliberately NOT set as `caused_by`

Of those 18 commits, exactly ONE touches both `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/reconcile.py`
and the failing test's own file `tests/interfaces/store/test_reconciler_apply_bindings.py`:

    a33333b8709a  "Remove reconciler internal shims"

which is also the exact `headSha` of the first red run.

That is strong circumstantial evidence, but it is **correlation, not experiment**: no bisect and
no revert test was run. I am therefore NOT recording a `caused_by` link, because doing so would
assert an attribution I have not proven. Anyone wanting it pinned can do so cheaply by reverting
that commit against the non-editable selection.

## A residual the fix does not depend on

The ticket's confirmed account explains the install-mode correlation (4/4: non-editable lanes
red, editable green) but does NOT by itself explain the TIMING — why lanes that require a
non-editable install were green at `e510c64dbcb6` and red at `a33333b8709a`. Both facts hold, so
the mechanism plausibly needs non-editable install AND something that landed in that window.

This residual does not undermine the fix or this close: the fix does not rely on the trigger's
identity. It patches `reconcile._runtime` — the object `reconcile.py:197` actually hands to
`bind_operation_runtime` — instead of loading a second `rebar_reconciler.runtime` by path, and
ships a regression test that manufactures the split-engine topology in ANY install mode. It is
therefore correct independently of which commit surfaced the latent divergence, and the lanes
are green on main. Recorded so the residual is visible rather than silently absorbed.
